questions.stem: A patient has an overactive thyroid gland, producing excess thyroxine. Which symptoms would you expect them to show?

options.text: Weight gain, feeling cold, and lethargy
Weight loss, increased heart rate, and feeling anxious or restless
Excessive thirst and frequent urination
Muscle cramps and brittle bones

questions.explanation: Thyroxine controls the basal metabolic rate. Excess thyroxine (hyperthyroidism) speeds up metabolism, causing weight loss, increased heart rate, restlessness, anxiety, and heat intolerance. The opposite symptoms (weight gain, lethargy) occur with too little thyroxine (hypothyroidism).

questions.stem: Thyroxine production is controlled by TSH from the pituitary gland. When thyroxine levels are high, TSH production decreases. What type of control mechanism is this?

options.text: Positive feedback — high thyroxine stimulates more TSH
Negative feedback — high thyroxine inhibits TSH release, reducing further thyroxine production
No feedback — TSH production is constant regardless of thyroxine levels
Positive feedback — TSH directly converts into thyroxine

questions.explanation: This is negative feedback: when thyroxine levels rise above normal, this inhibits the pituitary gland from producing TSH. Less TSH means the thyroid is less stimulated, so thyroxine production falls back to normal. When thyroxine drops, TSH increases again.

questions.stem: A doctor tests for hormone levels by taking a blood sample. Why is a blood sample the appropriate method to test hormone levels?

options.text: Hormones are only produced in the blood cells
Hormones are secreted into the blood by endocrine glands and transported to target organs, so blood concentration reflects hormone levels
Hormones are stored permanently in the blood plasma
Blood samples can detect the glands that produce the hormones

questions.explanation: Endocrine glands secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream, which transports them throughout the body. Measuring hormone concentration in the blood therefore gives an accurate indication of how much hormone is being produced and is circulating.

questions.stem: Testosterone is produced by the testes. During male puberty, testosterone levels rise significantly. Which changes are directly caused by testosterone?

options.text: Growth of the uterus lining and onset of menstruation
Deepening of the voice, growth of facial hair, and increased muscle mass
Development of mammary glands and widening of the hips
Increased production of FSH and LH only

questions.explanation: Testosterone is the main male sex hormone responsible for male secondary sexual characteristics during puberty: voice deepening, facial and body hair growth, increased muscle mass, and development of the male reproductive organs. The other options describe effects of female hormones.

questions.stem: Insulin and glucagon are both produced by the pancreas but have opposite effects. Why is it advantageous to have two hormones with opposing actions controlling blood glucose?

options.text: One hormone is for daytime and the other for nighttime
Having antagonistic hormones allows precise, fine-tuned control of blood glucose in both directions — up and down
The body cannot produce enough of one hormone, so it needs a backup
Insulin and glucagon cancel each other out so blood glucose stays constant without regulation

questions.explanation: Antagonistic hormones provide more precise control. If glucose is too high, insulin lowers it. If glucose is too low, glucagon raises it. This two-way control allows the body to rapidly and accurately correct deviations in either direction, maintaining glucose within a narrow, safe range.
